patient.name: Gary Whitfield
patient.complaint: Brought in by hostel staff: confused, unsteady and seeing double for 2 days
background: Drinks about a litre of vodka a day for 15 years
Lives in a hostel in Camden; eats very little
Two previous admissions with alcohol withdrawal
No regular medication; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a heavy drinker (or a starved, vomiting patient) who is confused, ataxic and has nystagmus or a lateral rectus palsy. Distractors are delirium tremens, hepatic encephalopathy and Korsakoff's.

points: Gary, 49, found wandering the hostel corridor, **confused**.
Staff say he has been **unsteady on his feet** for 2 days.
He keeps saying he is **seeing double**.
Last drink was this morning; he has barely eaten for weeks.

steps.lead: Gary's confusion, wobbly gait and double vision point to **thiamine (B1) deficiency** hitting the brain, especially the mamillary bodies.
Gary's **chronic alcohol use** and near-starvation are the commonest route to Wernicke's. In a non-drinker, look for hyperemesis, anorexia or malabsorption.

points: Eyes: he cannot look outwards with either eye (**bilateral lateral rectus palsy**).
Broad-based, **ataxic gait**; cannot walk heel to toe.
Reduced sensation in both feet (peripheral neuropathy).
No tremor, no sweating, no hallucinations; no asterixis.

steps.lead: Gary has the **full triad**, which only about 10% of patients show. Do not wait for all three: any one in a drinker is enough to treat.

steps.title: The classic triad
nodes: Any one in an at-risk patient → treat
steps.caption: Remember 'COAT': Confusion, Ophthalmoplegia, Ataxia, Thiamine.

steps.q: Gary is confused and ataxic with ophthalmoplegia, but not tremulous or hallucinating. Which is most likely?
steps.r: Eye signs plus ataxia plus acute confusion is **Wernicke's**. DTs give tremor, sweating and hallucinations; hepatic encephalopathy gives asterixis.

steps.lead: A drinker who is **confused and unsteady** is the presentation to recognise: Gary gets IV thiamine now, not after tests.
If Gary is not treated, he risks **Korsakoff's**: he would invent stories (confabulate) to fill gaps he cannot remember.

steps.text: Korsakoff's is the **chronic** end point (amnesia, confabulation). A patient who is **acutely** confused with eye signs and ataxia has Wernicke's, not Korsakoff's.

investigation.exam: Wernicke's is a **clinical diagnosis**, so investigation questions usually test that you do not delay treatment for an MRI or thiamine level, check a glucose first, and screen for alcohol dependence with CAGE.

steps.title: Gary's bloods in ED
steps.text: Macrocytosis and a high GGT fit heavy drinking. Normal glucose, sodium and ammonia make hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hepatic encephalopathy unlikely.

visual.title: Capillary glucose before treatment
visual.label: Gary 5.8
visual.caption: Always check the glucose first. Gary's is normal, so the next step is simply **IV thiamine**.

steps.lead: Gary's diagnosis is made at the bedside from his history and signs. An MRI could support it later but must **not delay** thiamine.

steps.q: The registrar wants a serum thiamine level before treating Gary. What is the best response?
o: Give IV thiamine now; diagnosis is clinical
steps.r: Wernicke's is a **clinical diagnosis**. Thiamine levels are not used acutely and waiting risks permanent Korsakoff's.

steps.lead: Once Gary is treated and calmer, the **CAGE** questions screen him for alcohol dependence and open the conversation about stopping.

visual.title: CAGE score
visual.label: Gary 4/4
visual.caption: Two or more 'yes' answers is clinically significant. Gary answers yes to all four, including the morning **eye-opener**.

steps.text: If an MRI is done, it shows signal change in the **mamillary bodies**, periaqueductal grey and medial thalami. Useful support, never a reason to delay treatment.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' in a confused, ataxic drinker: the answer is **IV thiamine (Pabrinex)**. The twist is hypoglycaemia: give glucose too, with thiamine alongside or before.

steps.q: Gary's glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
steps.r: **IV Pabrinex** treats the cause. Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in drinkers; glucose is not needed with a normal CBG.

steps.lead: Gary starts **IV Pabrinex** now and continues it for **5 days**. Any glucose-containing drip comes after the thiamine.

steps.title: Confused drinker in ED
nodes: Glucose low → IV 20% glucose with IV thiamine alongside or before
Then oral thiamine, nutrition and alcohol support
steps.caption: Correcting hypoglycaemia is never delayed, but thiamine goes in with it.

steps.lead: Had Gary's glucose been 2.4, the **20% glucose** comes first, with Pabrinex given alongside so the glucose does not tip him into worse Wernicke's.

steps.text: Do not give **IM glucagon** to a malnourished drinker: his liver glycogen is depleted, so it often fails. Give IV glucose.

visual.title: Gary's response to IV Pabrinex
visual.caption: Eye signs improve within hours to days; ataxia and memory recover slowly and may never fully return.

steps.lead: After 5 days, Gary moves to **oral thiamine**, a dietitian review and alcohol support. Stopping drinking is the real long-term treatment.
Gary's plan follows **RCP guidance** on Pabrinex in alcohol-related presentations, and the CAGE screen opens the route to alcohol services.

steps.text: Also watch Gary for **alcohol withdrawal** (a chlordiazepoxide regimen) and refeeding: they are separate problems that often travel with Wernicke's.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: which enzyme needs thiamine, why glucose without thiamine makes it worse, why alcohol causes deficiency, and why the mamillary bodies are hit.

steps.lead: Gary eats little, his gut absorbs thiamine poorly and his fatty liver stores little: **three hits** that empty a store that only lasts weeks.
Without thiamine, Gary's neurones cannot run **pyruvate dehydrogenase** or the Krebs cycle properly, so they run out of energy.

steps.title: From no thiamine to neuronal damage
nodes: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase fail
steps.caption: Transketolase (pentose phosphate pathway) also needs thiamine; its activity falls too.

steps.lead: Gary's **mamillary bodies** and periaqueductal grey burn energy fastest, so they fail first: this explains his eye signs, ataxia and the MRI pattern.
A dextrose drip before Pabrinex would push more glucose through pathways that **consume** Gary's last thiamine, and could make him worse.

steps.q: Why can IV dextrose without thiamine worsen Gary's condition?
o: It uses up remaining thiamine in glucose metabolism
steps.r: Thiamine is a cofactor in **glucose metabolism**, so a glucose load uses up what little is left.

steps.lead: If Gary had been missed, damage to the **mamillary bodies and thalamus** would become permanent: Korsakoff's amnesia that thiamine cannot reverse.

steps.text: **Anterograde** amnesia (cannot lay down new memories) is the core of Korsakoff's; confabulation fills the gaps.

mcq.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy?
mcq.r: Wernicke's is **thiamine (B1)** deficiency. Niacin deficiency is pellagra.

mcq.q: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
mcq.r: **Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.** Tremor, sweating and hallucinations are delirium tremens.

mcq.q: What proportion of patients present with the full triad?
What is the most important cause of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
mcq.r: **Chronic alcoholism** is the most important cause; the others are recognised causes too.

mcq.q: Which complication follows untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy?

mcq.r: It is a **clinical diagnosis**. MRI may support; thiamine levels are not used acutely.

mcq.q: Which tool screens for alcohol dependence in the notes?
How long is parenteral thiamine given in confirmed Wernicke's?
mcq.r: IV Pabrinex for **5 days**, then oral thiamine.

mcq.q: A suspected Wernicke's patient has a glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. What do you do?
o: Give IV 20% glucose with IV thiamine
Give thiamine, then wait 1 hour for glucose
mcq.r: Hypoglycaemia is corrected **now**, with thiamine given alongside or before.

mcq.q: Which enzyme uses thiamine as a cofactor?
mcq.r: **Pyruvate dehydrogenase**, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase need thiamine.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his partner because he has been confused and unsteady for 3 days. He drinks around 15 cans of strong lager a day and has lost weight. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. He has horizontal nystagmus and cannot abduct either eye. His gait is broad-based. There is no tremor or asterixis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a confused drinker: sort Wernicke's, withdrawal, liver and Korsakoff's.

clues: 15 cans of strong lager a day
steps.x: Heavy drinking and weight loss = thiamine risk. Bilateral lateral rectus palsy, nystagmus, ataxia and confusion = the triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in a drinker: **Wernicke's encephalopathy**.

elim: Withdrawal gives tremor, sweating and agitation; there is no tremor.
A bleed is sudden with headache and vomiting, not bilateral sixth nerve palsies.
Hepatic encephalopathy gives asterixis and jaundice; asterixis is absent.
Korsakoff's is chronic amnesia with confabulation, not acute eye signs.

steps.x: **E. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Rule: drinker + confusion + eye signs + ataxia = Wernicke's until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department confused. She drinks a bottle of wine a day and has eaten little for weeks. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. She has nystagmus and an ataxic gait. The doctor suspects Wernicke's encephalopathy and wants to start treatment.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation before treatment: the bedside test that changes the next step.
A starved, confused drinker may be **hypoglycaemic**, which changes the order of treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check a **capillary glucose**: if low, give 20% glucose with thiamine; if normal, IV thiamine.

elim: CT head does not diagnose Wernicke's and would delay treatment.
No meningism or fever; LP is not indicated.
MRI may support later but is not required and must not delay thiamine.
Thiamine levels are not used acutely.

steps.x: **A. Capillary blood glucose.** Rule: Wernicke's is clinical; the glucose decides what goes in first.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man with alcohol dependence is found drowsy and confused at home. He is ataxic and has bilateral lateral rectus palsy. His pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and GCS 13. His capillary blood glucose is 2.3 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management in a confused drinker with a lab result: look at the glucose.
Wernicke's features plus **hypoglycaemia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Correct the hypoglycaemia now with **IV 20% glucose**, giving **IV thiamine** alongside so glucose does not worsen Wernicke's.

elim: Glucagon often fails in drinkers with depleted liver glycogen.
Saline treats neither the hypoglycaemia nor the thiamine deficiency.
Chlordiazepoxide treats withdrawal, not hypoglycaemia or Wernicke's.
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed and too slow; IV is needed.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: hypoglycaemia is corrected first, but thiamine goes in alongside or before the glucose.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man who drinks heavily is admitted with vomiting. He is given intravenous 5% dextrose overnight. The next morning he is newly confused, has nystagmus and cannot walk unaided. He has not received any vitamins.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for his deterioration?
o: Increased thiamine consumption by glucose metabolism

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain why he got worse after dextrose.

clues: newly confused, has nystagmus and cannot walk unaided
steps.x: A thiamine-depleted drinker given glucose without thiamine now has the Wernicke's triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiamine is a cofactor in **glucose metabolism**; the glucose load used up his last thiamine.

elim: Overnight 5% dextrose rarely causes cerebral oedema, and would not give nystagmus and ataxia.
Osmotic diuresis needs marked hyperglycaemia and causes dehydration, not eye signs.
Osmotic demyelination follows rapid sodium correction, not dextrose.
Rebound hypoglycaemia does not explain nystagmus and ataxia.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's.

practice.stem: A 54 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by hostel staff. He has been confused for 2 days and keeps falling. He drinks a litre of vodka daily. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. He has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based gait. There is no flap.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus in a heavy drinker is Wernicke's. Normal ammonia and no flap argue against hepatic encephalopathy; normal glucose excludes hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a confused drinker: use the bloods to rule out mimics.
Confusion + ataxia + eye signs in a drinker. MCV and GGT confirm heavy drinking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wernicke's encephalopathy**.

elim: Withdrawal causes tremor, sweating and agitation, not nystagmus and ataxia.
A bleed is sudden with headache; 2 days of confusion and nystagmus fit Wernicke's better.
No flap and a normal ammonia.
Glucose is 5.4 mmol/L.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: the normal glucose and ammonia are there to remove the mimics.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman who is 11 weeks pregnant has had severe vomiting for 4 weeks and has lost 6 kg. She is now confused and unsteady and reports double vision. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. She has nystagmus on lateral gaze and a wide-based gait.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her neurological symptoms?
practice.e: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a recognised cause of Wernicke's: confusion, ataxia and eye signs mean thiamine deficiency. Her electrolytes are normal.

steps.x: Asks for the cause of neurological symptoms in a pregnant woman with vomiting.
**Hyperemesis gravidarum** starves her of thiamine; she now has the triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wernicke's from **thiamine deficiency**.

elim: Potassium is normal.
Sodium is normal.
Venous sinus thrombosis causes headache, seizures and papilloedema, not this triad.
B12 deficiency is slow, with neuropathy and dorsal column signs, not acute ophthalmoplegia.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: Wernicke's is not only alcohol; think hyperemesis, anorexia and malabsorption.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man who drinks heavily is admitted confused and ataxic. He says everything looks doubled when he looks to either side. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his eyes?
practice.e: Ophthalmoplegia in Wernicke's is classically bilateral lateral rectus (sixth nerve) palsy with nystagmus. Bitemporal hemianopia is a pituitary sign.

steps.x: Most likely eye finding in Wernicke's.

clues: doubled when he looks to either side
steps.x: Horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze to both sides = both eyes cannot abduct.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bilateral lateral rectus palsy**.

elim: Bitemporal hemianopia is chiasmal compression, e.g. pituitary tumour.
Horner's is a sympathetic lesion: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.
Papilloedema means raised intracranial pressure.
RAPD is an optic nerve sign, e.g. optic neuritis.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: the 'ophthalmoplegia' of Wernicke's is lateral rectus palsy plus nystagmus.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man was treated for Wernicke's encephalopathy 6 months ago but continued drinking. His sister says he cannot remember conversations from earlier in the day. When asked what he did this morning, he describes a detailed trip to the seaside that did not happen. He is alert and his eye movements are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Anterograde amnesia with confabulation after Wernicke's is Korsakoff's syndrome, from irreversible mamillary body and thalamic damage.

steps.x: A diagnosis after previous Wernicke's: think about its complication.

clues: treated for Wernicke's encephalopathy 6 months ago
cannot remember conversations from earlier in the day
trip to the seaside that did not happen
steps.x: Anterograde amnesia plus **confabulation** in an alert patient after Wernicke's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Korsakoff's syndrome**.

elim: Alzheimer's is gradual global decline in an older person, without this history.
DTs is acute withdrawal with tremor and hallucinations; he is alert and calm.
TGA is a single episode lasting hours, without confabulation.
Vascular dementia is stepwise with vascular risk factors and focal signs.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: confabulation after Wernicke's = Korsakoff's.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman who drinks heavily is confused on the ward. The nurse asks the doctor to check her gait, which has become worse since admission. Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her gait?
practice.e: Wernicke's causes cerebellar-type ataxia: a broad-based, unsteady gait. Festinating gait is Parkinson's.

steps.x: Most likely gait finding in Wernicke's.
Ataxia is part of the triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Broad-based ataxic gait**.

elim: Festinating gait is Parkinson's disease.
High-stepping gait is foot drop, e.g. common peroneal palsy.
Scissoring gait is spastic paraparesis.
Waddling gait is proximal myopathy.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: the 'A' of the triad is a wide-based, unsteady gait.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 13.5 kg/m2. Two days later she becomes confused and unsteady and has nystagmus on looking to either side. Her temperature is 36.1°C, pulse rate 52 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Starvation from anorexia nervosa causes thiamine deficiency; acute confusion, ataxia and nystagmus are Wernicke's. Glucose and sodium are normal.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a severely underweight patient with new neurology.

clues: nystagmus on looking to either side
steps.x: Prolonged starvation is a recognised cause; she has the triad features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wernicke's encephalopathy**.

elim: A tumour is gradual, with headache; this came on over days in a starved patient.
Glucose is 4.4 mmol/L.
Sodium is 138 mmol/L.
MS does not cause acute confusion like this, and her risk is starvation.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: any starved patient with confusion, ataxia or eye signs needs IV thiamine.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man is recovering on the ward after 5 days of intravenous Pabrinex for Wernicke's encephalopathy. He admits he finds it hard to stop drinking and has a drink first thing in the morning to steady his nerves. The team wants to screen him for alcohol dependence.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: CAGE screens for alcohol dependence; two or more yes answers is significant. AMTS and MMSE test cognition; GAD-7 and PHQ-9 screen anxiety and depression.

steps.x: A screening test for alcohol dependence.

clues: drink first thing in the morning
steps.x: The morning drink is the CAGE 'eye-opener'.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CAGE questionnaire**.

elim: AMTS screens cognition, not alcohol use.
GAD-7 screens for anxiety.
MMSE assesses cognition.
PHQ-9 screens for depression.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with alcohol dependence was started on intravenous Pabrinex for confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. His eye signs improved but his memory remains poor. The neurologist requests imaging to look for changes supporting Wernicke's encephalopathy.
practice.q: Which investigation is most likely to show supporting changes?
practice.e: MRI brain can show signal change in the mamillary bodies, periaqueductal grey and medial thalami. It supports but is not required; CT is insensitive.

steps.x: Which test shows changes that support the diagnosis (after treatment started).
Treatment has not been delayed; now supporting imaging is wanted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain**: mamillary body changes.

elim: CT is insensitive for the small mamillary body changes.
EEG is for seizures; it is not imaging and is non-specific here.
LP is for infection or bleeding.
Nerve conduction studies assess his neuropathy, not the brain.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: MRI supports, but Wernicke's is clinical and treatment never waits for it.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department confused and unsteady. He drinks heavily and has double vision. His pulse rate is 106 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and GCS 14. He has nystagmus and bilateral lateral rectus palsy. His capillary blood glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Suspected Wernicke's with a normal glucose: give IV thiamine (Pabrinex) now. Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed; imaging must not delay treatment.

steps.x: Initial management; check the glucose first.
Full triad and a **normal glucose**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV Pabrinex** straight away.

elim: Glucose is normal, and glucose before thiamine could worsen Wernicke's.
Diagnosis is clinical; scanning first delays treatment.
Folate does not treat thiamine deficiency.
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in drinkers and too slow acutely.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: suspected Wernicke's = IV (parenteral) thiamine now.

practice.stem: A 51 year old woman with alcohol dependence was diagnosed with Wernicke's encephalopathy yesterday and given intravenous Pabrinex. Her nystagmus has already improved. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. The ward team asks how long to continue parenteral thiamine.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of parenteral thiamine?
practice.e: In confirmed Wernicke's, parenteral thiamine continues for 5 days, then oral thiamine. Stopping when the eye signs improve is a classic error.

steps.x: Duration of IV thiamine in confirmed Wernicke's.

clues: how long to continue parenteral thiamine
steps.x: Early improvement does not mean stop.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **5 days** of parenteral thiamine.

elim: One day is far too short; eye signs improve first but the rest does not.
Three days is too short for confirmed Wernicke's.
Two weeks of IV is unnecessary; switch to oral after 5 days.
Six weeks of IV is not standard.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: confirmed Wernicke's = parenteral thiamine for 5 days.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man has completed 5 days of intravenous Pabrinex for Wernicke's encephalopathy. He is malnourished and plans to keep drinking, though he will see the alcohol team. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. He is being discharged.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Ongoing harmful drinking with malnourishment needs oral thiamine, plus treating the cause: alcohol support and nutrition.

steps.x: Long-term management after the IV course.
Harmful drinking plus malnourishment = indication for oral thiamine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral thiamine** with alcohol cessation and nutritional support.

elim: B12 injections treat pernicious anaemia, not thiamine deficiency.
He remains at high risk of recurrence.
Folate alone does not replace thiamine.
Vitamin D does not address his thiamine risk.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: after IV, oral thiamine for drinkers who are malnourished, plus treat the cause.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man with alcohol dependence develops confusion, ataxia and nystagmus. His blood lactate is raised despite a normal blood pressure. The team explains that a vitamin he lacks is a cofactor in cerebral glucose metabolism.
practice.q: Which enzyme is most likely to have reduced activity?
practice.e: Thiamine is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase; when it fails, pyruvate is shunted to lactate. Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin.

steps.x: A mechanism question: which thiamine-dependent enzyme fails.
Wernicke's (thiamine deficiency) plus lactate build-up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pyruvate dehydrogenase** (also alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase).

elim: Glucose-6-phosphatase is in gluconeogenesis and needs no thiamine.
Hexokinase does not need thiamine.
LDH is working; it makes the extra lactate.
Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: thiamine enzymes are PDH, alpha-KGDH and transketolase.

prompts.q: What is Wernicke's encephalopathy and which brain area is classically affected?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the vitamin with its number and the structure.

points.p: Acute neurological condition from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
points.why: Not B12: that causes subacute combined degeneration.
Also periaqueductal grey and medial thalami.

prompts.q: Who gets Wernicke's encephalopathy? Name the causes.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem may hide a pregnant vomiter or an anorexic patient, not a drinker.

points.why: The commonest cause by far.
Thiamine stores last only a few weeks.
A classic non-alcohol stem.
Any cause of poor absorption counts.

prompts.q: What is the classic triad, and how often is it complete?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one feature in an at-risk patient is enough to treat.

points.why: Acute, often with drowsiness.
Broad-based, cerebellar-type gait.

points.p: Ophthalmoplegia, e.g. bilateral lateral rectus palsy
points.why: Nystagmus is also common.
Waiting for the full triad misses most cases.

prompts.q: Which other features are common besides the triad?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these support the diagnosis in an incomplete presentation.

points.why: The commonest eye sign.
Can progress to Korsakoff's.
Reflects thiamine and alcohol damage to nerves.

prompts.q: How do you tell Wernicke's from Korsakoff's syndrome, and what defines Korsakoff's?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: acute and eye signs = Wernicke's; chronic and confabulating = Korsakoff's.

points.p: Korsakoff's is the result of untreated Wernicke's
points.why: Prevented by early IV thiamine.
Anterograde loss is the core feature.
Filling memory gaps with invented stories.
With a clear level of consciousness.

prompts.q: How is Wernicke's diagnosed, and what is the role of MRI and thiamine levels?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: any answer that delays thiamine for a test is wrong.

points.why: History plus signs.

points.p: MRI brain may support but is not required
points.why: Shows mamillary body change.
Results take too long and do not change management.

prompts.q: Which screening tool is used for alcohol dependence, and what are its four questions?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'eye-opener' is often hidden in the stem.

points.why: Two or more yes answers is significant.
Felt you should cut down?
Annoyed by criticism? Guilty about drinking?
Drink first thing in the morning.

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment, for how long, and when relative to glucose?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the answer is IV, not oral, thiamine.

points.p: IV thiamine (Pabrinex, B and C vitamins)
points.why: Oral is poorly absorbed in drinkers.

points.p: Parenterally for 5 days in confirmed Wernicke's
points.why: Then switch to oral.
Glucose first can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's.

prompts.q: A suspected Wernicke's patient is hypoglycaemic. What do you do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: never leave hypoglycaemia untreated to wait for thiamine.

points.p: Give 20% glucose IV: correcting hypoglycaemia takes priority
points.why: Glucagon often fails in malnourished drinkers.

points.p: Give thiamine alongside or before the glucose
points.why: To avoid precipitating Wernicke's.

prompts.q: What is the long-term management after the IV course?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat the cause, not just the vitamin level.

points.p: Oral thiamine if harmful drinking with malnourishment, decompensated liver disease or assisted withdrawal
points.why: These groups stay at high risk.

points.p: Supportive care: fluids and nutritional support
points.why: Watch for refeeding.
Removes the cause.

prompts.q: Why does thiamine deficiency damage neurones, and why are the mamillary bodies hit?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the three enzymes.

points.why: Links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
Krebs cycle and pentose phosphate pathway.
Impaired cerebral glucose metabolism.

points.p: Mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey have high metabolic turnover
points.why: So they fail first.

prompts.q: Why do drinkers become thiamine deficient, and why can glucose without thiamine worsen things?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three reasons for deficiency, one for the glucose effect.

points.why: Calories come from alcohol.
Alcohol impairs gut uptake.
A damaged liver stores little.

points.p: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine, depleting stores further
points.why: Hence thiamine before or with glucose.

glossary.Wernicke's encephalopathy: Acute brain dysfunction caused by thiamine deficiency, classically confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.
glossary.Korsakoff's syndrome: Chronic, largely irreversible amnesia with confabulation following untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.
glossary.Korsakoff's: Short for Korsakoff's syndrome: chronic amnesia and confabulation after untreated Wernicke's.
glossary.thiamine: Vitamin B1; a cofactor for key enzymes of glucose metabolism.
glossary.Pabrinex: Intravenous high-dose B vitamins (including thiamine) and vitamin C, used to treat or prevent Wernicke's.
glossary.mamillary bodies: Small paired structures under the brain, part of the memory circuit, damaged in Wernicke's and Korsakoff's.
glossary.periaqueductal grey: Grey matter around the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain; often affected in Wernicke's.
glossary.ataxia: Lack of coordination, here a broad-based unsteady gait.
glossary.ophthalmoplegia: Weakness or paralysis of the eye muscles, causing impaired eye movements and double vision.
glossary.lateral rectus: Eye muscle that moves the eye outwards; supplied by the sixth cranial nerve.
glossary.nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic jerking of the eyes.
glossary.confabulation: Unintentionally making up false memories to fill gaps in memory.
glossary.anterograde amnesia: Inability to form new memories after the brain injury.
glossary.retrograde amnesia: Loss of memories formed before the brain injury.
glossary.peripheral neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves, causing numbness or tingling, usually in the feet first.
glossary.CAGE: Four-question alcohol dependence screen: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; two or more yes answers is significant.
glossary.eye-opener: An alcoholic drink first thing in the morning to steady nerves or ease withdrawal.
glossary.hyperemesis gravidarum: Severe, persistent vomiting in pregnancy causing dehydration, weight loss or electrolyte problems.
glossary.anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder with deliberate restriction of intake and very low body weight.
glossary.malabsorption: Poor absorption of nutrients from the gut.
glossary.delirium tremens: Severe alcohol withdrawal 48 to 72 hours after the last drink with tremor, sweating and hallucinations.
glossary.hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion caused by liver failure and raised ammonia; asterixis is a key sign.
glossary.asterixis: A flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, seen in liver or respiratory failure.
glossary.pyruvate dehydrogenase: Thiamine-dependent enzyme converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
glossary.transketolase: Thiamine-dependent enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway.
glossary.chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to manage alcohol withdrawal.
glossary.glucagon: Hormone that raises glucose by releasing liver glycogen; often ineffective in malnourished drinkers.
glossary.macrocytosis: Red cells larger than normal (raised MCV), common with heavy alcohol use.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: the average size of red blood cells.
glossary.GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase: a liver enzyme raised by heavy alcohol use.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale: scores eye, verbal and motor response from 3 to 15.
glossary.CBG: Capillary blood glucose: a finger-prick glucose test.
glossary.refeeding syndrome: Dangerous shifts in phosphate, potassium and magnesium when a starved patient starts eating again.
glossary.thalamus: Central brain relay station; medial thalamic damage contributes to Korsakoff's amnesia.
